title: Photosynthesis
note: Photosynthesis runs in two linked stages in the chloroplast. The light-dependent reactions on the thylakoid membranes split water, release O2, and make ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle in the stroma spends that ATP and NADPH to fix CO2 into sugar.

read.title: Two stages, one chloroplast
text: Inside a leaf cell, each chloroplast contains stacks of flattened membrane sacs called thylakoids, surrounded by a fluid called the stroma. The two stages of photosynthesis divide the work between these spaces.

The light-dependent reactions happen in the thylakoid membranes. Pigments, mainly chlorophyll, absorb blue and red light and funnel the energy to a reaction center. In photosystem II, excited electrons leave the reaction center and are replaced by electrons pulled from water. Splitting water releases oxygen gas. The electrons travel down a transport chain that pumps hydrogen ions into the thylakoid interior, then photosystem I boosts them again so they can reduce NADP+ to NADPH. The hydrogen ions flow back out through ATP synthase, making ATP.

The Calvin cycle runs in the stroma. The enzyme RuBisCO attaches CO2 to a five-carbon sugar, RuBP. The resulting molecules are reduced, using ATP and NADPH, into a three-carbon sugar, G3P. For every three CO2 fixed, one G3P leaves the cycle to be built into glucose and other molecules; the rest are rearranged, with more ATP, to regenerate RuBP.
Light reactions make the energy carriers; the Calvin cycle spends them. Neither stage can keep going for long without the other.
